In trade war with US, China’s bold stance hides
economic and political anxieties
articles.body_raw:
larly targeted American allies and partners -
directly waming the Europeans against “ap-
peasement” of the US while talking about “re-
gional economic integration” and restarting
negotiations ona trilateral free trade agree-
ment with Japan and South Korea.
Meanwhile, the Chinese have argued
that Trump's rollback on tariffs on the rest
of the world is an attempt to revive eco-
nomicblocs and spheres of influence. While
China professes its opposition to this and
proclaims itself a champion of globalisation,
a world divided into blocs is not necessarily
a bad thing for Beijing. To try and take over
global hegemony from the US without
some degree of open contest or confronta-
tion was always going to be a long shot for
China’s rulers, Therefore, a world divided,
where it is clearly the leader of one bloc, is
the next best option for China.
In April, a Chinese Ministry of
Commerce spokesperson while stating ex-
plicitly that “China and the US are not in
talks ontariffs”, also said that “the US needs
to show sincerity if it wants to talk... The
US should revoke all unilateral tariffs on
China if it wants to solve problems.”
That Beijing should at all refer to talks
with the US suggests that the assertive lan-
guage masks other concerns. Communist
Party of China (CPC) general secretary and
Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting at
the end of March with the heads of over
40 global corporations, including
American ones, as well as Premier Li
Qiang’s announcement in mid-April of
measures to support exporters and incen-
tivise MNCs to keep investing in China,
might suggest an attempt to make use of
opportunities created by the trade war.
This also explains Xi’s recent visits to
Southeast Asia and, no doubt, the sudden
desire to improve India-China ties with
references to a “dragon-elephant tango”.
Other measures, however, suggest con-
cems about the fallout of the trade war do-
mestically — steps have been announced, for

example, to help businesses keep workers
on their payrolls and stimulate private sec-
tor investment. Itis not surprising, then, that
a Chinese White Paper on the trade war and
other statements have been at pains to por-
tray how useful bilateral trade has been for
the American economy and consumers.
Clearly, forthe Chinese, as everywhere else,
external challenges take a distant second
place tomore immediate domestic concems.
Youth unemployment has hit historic
highs in China while the Covid pandemic
was a spectacular failure of political ac-
countability. The continuing anti-corrup-
tion campaign, meanwhile, suggests that
the Augean stables of China's ad ministra-
tion are far from being cleansed.
It has not been easy for the CPC to get its
people, particularly the youth, on board its
domestic projects of “national rejuvena-
tion”. Consider such trends as tang ping or
“lying flat” — a reaction against the long
hours of work expected from young
Chinese for ever-decreasing monetary re-
turns or job satisfaction — or the lack of con-
sumer confidence that continues to prevent
the Chinese economy from executing a full
post-pandemic economic recovery.
Before the Trump tariffs, most Chinese
possibly blamed the CPC and its leadership
for their problems. The Chinese leadership
might now be trying to use the opportunity
to spina narrative of standing up to what it
has called the bullying behaviour by the US.
However, political exhortation and at-
tempts to milk the tariff war with the US,
whether for external or domestic political
objectives, will have its limits. Eventually,
they will reflect not so much China’s re-
silience as the Chinese leadership's ability to
deflect blame.

The writer is associate professor,
Department of International Relations and
Governance Studies, and director, Centre of
Excellence for Himalayan Studies, Shiv
Nadar University, Delhi NCR

That government has started formally mapping capex by private
sector is welcome. It will help policymakers, corporations
T HE MINISTRY OF Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSP1) has re-
leased the first ever “Forward-Looking Survey on Private Sector CAPEX
Investment Intentions”. Capex refers to capital expenditure, which means
money spent towards the creation of long-term productive assets in the
economy. As the survey underscores, “capex is fundamental to expanding production
capacity, thereby serving as a catalyst for accelerated economic growth. This growth, in
turn, supports job creation and enhances labour productivity.” For a developing econ-
omy such as India, a high growth rate in capex is central to achieving the ambition of be-
coming a prosperous nation and transitioning into a developed country. The survey was
conducted between November 2024 and January 2025. The primary objective of this
survey is to estimate the capex trends of private corporate sector enterprises for five years:
From the past three financial years (2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24, in the current in-
stance) along with anticipated capital expenditure for the current year(2024-25, in this
instance) and the upcoming financial year(2025-26).
Out of a total of 3,064 responding enterprises, only 2,172 reported their capex data
(actual and intentions) for the full five-year period. Even though the survey was con-
ducted under the Collection of Statistics Act, 2008, MoSPI noted that many companies had
reservations about sharing data, thanks to concerns relating to legitimacy and cyber-
risks. As a result, even MoSPI advises caution when reading the data. “As this is the first
round of the survey, the findings may be seen as indicative and subject to refinement in
future iterations,” it says. On the whole, the datashows sharp fluctuations in private capex
from one year to another — varying from Rs 3.9 trillion in FY22 to Rs5.7 trillion in FY23,
then falling to Rs 4.2 trillion in FY24 before rising to Rs 6.6 trillion in FY25 and then falling
toaslowasRs 4.9 trillionin FY26. The year-on-year variations are so substantial that one
can draw very different conclusions based on the year chosen for analysis. For instance,
between FY22 and FY25, the capex grew by 66 per cent, but if you add the current year
(FY26), the overall growth fell to 23 per cent.
Even so, the survey underscores the existing notion that private sector capex has not
grown fast enough. The Union government's capex, for instance, grew by230 per cent in
the five years between FY21 and FY25. The government under Prime Minister Narendra
Modi has been trying to incentivise private sector capex because it believes that only
when the private sector starts investing can India make the economic transition. To that
end, it isa welcome move that the government has now started formally mapping capex
by the private sector. In the coming years, it will further help policymakers and corpora-
tions in making better choices,

“IF WARIS what the US wants, be it a tariff
war, a trade war or any other type of war,
we're ready to fight till the end.” So declared
a Chinese Foreign Ministry tweet in March
when the Donald Trump administration
raised tariffs over China’s lack of coopera-
tion in stemming the illegal flow of the opi-
oid fentanyl into the US.
The strong language coming out of
Beijing, coupled with the general percep-
tion of American policy being unstable or
reversible, has allowed a narrative to quickly
gain ground — not least in India — that
American President Donald Trump is the
one most likely to blink first.
However, while China certainly has the
state capacity to not only weather the storm
but to exploit it to its advantage, its frailties
are no less significant.
The Trump tariffs are certainly an op-
portunity for Beijing to make a case for
global leadership in the face of an unreli-
able and isolationist US. By describing
Trump as “a businessman by nature”, used
to cost-benefit analyses but incapable of
long-term strategic planning, China is do-
ing two things. One, it is running down
Trump the individual and, by extension, the
American system that produced him. Two,
it is making acase for a strategy of respond-
ing to pressure with pressure, and arguing
that showing weakness will only invite fur-
ther pressure.
In the bilateral context, Beijing is thus
using the Trump tariffs to legitimise and
bring out in the open its decades-long strat-
egy of countering American ingress into the
Chinese market and to strengthen its poli-
cies of self-reliance.

Letter by Manipur MLAs on need fora popular government
draws attention toa stalemate waiting to be broken in the stat
articles.body_raw:
draws attention toa stalemate waiting to be broken in the state
TT HE DECISION TO impose President's Rule in Manipur on February 13 followed
a failure to reach a consensus within the BJP on who would replace N Biren
Singh as chief minister. Singh had resigned four days earlier, after dissident BJP
MLAsstarted putting pressure on him to step down. On the one hand, his exit
was seen as a necessary step for anew start, while also being an implicit admission of his
inability to curtail the violence between the Meiteis and the Kukis. On the other hand, the
BJP in Manipur was, reportedly, against President’s Rule, arguably because that would
mean giving the Centre a greater role in the state. The opposition to its prolongation has
become more pronounced, with a group of 21 Manipur MLAs of the NDA submitting let-
ters to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah on April 29, asking
for a popular government to be installed in the state. The letter claims that even after al-
most three months of President's Rule, there have been “no visible actions to bring peace
and normalcy in the state”. The fact is that in twoyears of conflict, at least250 people have
died and thousands continue to languish in relief camps across the state.
It is true that there has been alull in the violence between the Meiteis and the Kukis.
Barring some clashes between security forces and civilians, an uneasy peace has pre-
vailed in most parts of the state since the escalation in November last year in Imphal West,
Bishnupur and Jiribam districts. But Manipur is far from a return to normalcy. There has
been nomeaningful political dialogue. Members of both communities still cannot return
home, and live without fear or prejudice. Highways remain blocked, and there has been
minimal disarmament and demilitarisation, despite Governor Ajay Kumar Bhalla’s ulti-
matum to militants, less than a week into President's Rule, to surrender their weapons.
The situation demands a restoration of the political process that can bring all sides to
the negotiating table. The larger goal is to restore trust between the Meitei and Kukicom-
munities, While a return of a popular government in the state is urgent and desirable,
the Centre must also prioritise confidence-building measures and consult with all the
stakeholders, The last thing Manipurneeds is a resurgence of gun violence and rioting that
would undo the fragile calm of the past several weeks.

to deepen collaboration in the space. Saudi
Arabia and Indiarecognise that the future be-
longs to nations investing not only in infra-
structure, but in building ecosystems where
technology, creativity, and talent intersect.
Under the leadership of Crown Prince
Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister
Modi, our countries are uniquely aligned in
this belief. As we showcase our unified gam-
ing strategy at WAVES, our message is one of
partnership and possibility. We are demon-
strating how government support, private in-
vestment, and global cooperation can work
together. Saudi Arabiais excited to collaborate
with India and other innovators toshape afu-
ture where gaming and esports reflect the di-
versity and ambition of the Global South.
Achieving these bold ambitions requires
notonly investment in dollars but also invest-
ment inpeople. At the Saudi Esports Federation
(SEF), which I have the privilege to chair, we
are building a platform where gaming drives
youth innovation and career growth. We are
proud that women now comprise nearly half
of Saudi’s gaming community, with pro-
grammes ensuring their full participation.
What sets apart Saudi Arabia's approach
is the unity across our gaming ecosystem —
goverment, federations, investors, and pri-
vate sector working together to meet Vision
2030 goals, This coordination reflectsa deeper
understanding that esports today sits at the
intersection of technology, innovation, and
entertainment — three pillars that also define
India's ambition, as showcased at WAVES.
Our collaboration extends globally
through the Global Esports Federation and
International Esports Federation, where I
proudly serve as vice president and president.

Saudi Arabia offers Indian developers a sup-
portive launchpad and attracts gamers from
across the Middle East, whileour growing in-
frastructure provides Indian esports teams
world-class venues, fuelling greater regional
competition and collaboration.
Ultimately, the story we are writing in
Saudi Arabia is not just about one country’s
rise in gaming; it is about how collaboration
and vision can unlock the potential of a gam-
ing industry, turning esports into a platform
for cross-cultural innovation and leadership.
We invite our friends in India and around the
world to join us in building an ecosystem
where innovation thrives; where economic,
social, and cultural benefits are shared by all.
The coming years will be transformative.
The global games industry is projected to reach
$600 billion by 2030, and emerging markets
like ours willbe key diivers. SaudiArabiaisin-
vesting heavily to contribute to and benefit
from this expansion, but collaboration is the
comerstone ofourapproach. We hopeourex-
perience offers insights to India’s policymakers
and industry leaders in nurturing a booming
creative economy. ToIndia’s gamers and pub-
lic, we extend an invitation — join our events,
play in our tournaments, and help shape the
future of gaming. Together, we can build a
more innovative and inclusive gaming world.
In the spirit of WAVES 2025, let us cele-
brate this new era ofentertainment andwork
collectively to ensure the gaming revolution
benefits communities everywhere.

The writer is chairman,

In Saudi Arabia, we have seen how games can bridge cultures and create opportunities. Guided by HRH the Crown Prince's Vision 2030, we are fostering a unified, nationwide gaming strategy. Itis apparent from the scaleand thematic expanse of WAVES that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has a similar vision. As such, the summit marks a timely opportunity to deepen ties between our countries and shape a future led by new voices andalliances, Under the guidance of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia views games and esports as key pillars of our future economy. Our National Gaming andEsports Strategy, launched in 2022, aims to transform the Kingdom into a leading global hub by 2030, with concrete goals including over 39,000 jobs, a $13-billion GDP contribution, and more than 100 professional teams already active among our 21 million gamers.One of our flagship initiatives, the Esports Worid Cup, announced by His Royal Highness Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in 2023, debutedin Riyadh with 200clubs, 1,500 athletes, two million visitors, and 500 million viewers. Beyond competition, the Esports World Cup symbolises how innovation, investment, and international collaboration can come together to shape a thriving, future-focused industry. This goal of nurturing global parmerships is reflected in gatherings like the WAVES Summit and events such as the New Global Sport Conference (NGSC), returning in 2025

As we showcase our unified gaming strategy at WAVES, our message is one of partnership and possibility. We are demonstrating how government support, private investment, and global cooperation can work together. Saudi Arabia is excited to collaborate with India and other innovators to shape a future where gaming and esports reflect the diversity and ambition of the Global South.

tury on the grand stage of the Indian Premier League. Only a teenager, mind
uncluttered by the pressure of expectations and unshackled by the game’s
conventions, could have imagined and then composed this stunning stroke-play. It may
be that Suryavanshi himself will fail toreproduce this effort. Whatis certain is that his life
and career will never be the same again.
The feats — the youngest to score a hundred in the format, the second-fastest centu-

flicted on a brigade of high-class, highly experienced bowlers. Ishant Sharma was five
years past his Test debut when Suryavanshi was born; Mohammed Siraj had already
caught the eye of veteran scouts in local leagues; Rashid Khan is the most successful
bowler in this format. The pedigree of the bowlers didn’t scare him, the grandness of the
stage didn’t subdue him, and the task of hunting down a steep target of 210 didn’t make
him flinch. How he reached this stage is also a fascinating story. Born in the cricketing
backwater of Tajpur in Samastipur district in Bihar, which has multiple cricketing asso-
Ciations feuding for power, his father sold his farmland tonurture his son's ambitions. He

game getting younger, the poster boy of a brave new world of cricketers. The crew of

minds and limitless ambitions, This is not the time to wonder where destiny will even-
tually lead him — to the summit of glory or the valley of unfulfilled renown. Itis the time
to marvelat his wondrous gifts, of both mind and bat.
